newsitem.title: USA: Clinton lauds Deng as "extraordinary figure".
newsitem.headline: Clinton lauds Deng as "extraordinary figure".

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Wednesday he was saddened to learn of the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, calling him an "extraordinary figure on the world stage over the past two decades."

In a statement issued during a visit to Boston, Clinton said he was saddened to learn of the death of Deng and described him as "the driving force behind China's decision to formalise relations with the United States."
Deng, who had been in failing health, died on Wednesday at the age of 93 from complications from Parkinson's disease and a lung infection.
Clinton said Deng's 1979 visit to America had laid the foundation for a rapid expansion of relations and cooperation between the two countries.
Clinton, then governor of Arkansas, met Deng during that visit when the Chinese leader attended a National Governors' Association meeting in Atlanta to discuss trade with China.

"Mr. Deng's long life spanned a century of turmoil, tribulation and remarkable change in China," said Clinton, who was informed of Deng's death by his staff while he was having lunch in Boston with local officials.
"He spurred China's historic economic reform programme, which greatly improved living standards in China and modernised much of the nation," Clinton said.
He added: "China today plays an important role in world affairs in no small part because of Mr.Deng's decision to open his country to the outside world."

Clinton, who dropped a confrontational approach toward Beijing that he espoused before being elected to his first term in 1992, is pursuing closer ties with China based on engaging the Asian giant rather than isolating it.

Although still pressing Beijing's communist leaders to improve human rights, the U.S. government is concentrating on building up trade and economic ties and says it hopes to encourage a more open, democratic society there.

"The continued emergence of China as a great power that is stable politically and open economically, that respects human rights and the rule of law and that becomes a full partner in building a secure international order is profoundly in America's interest and in the world's interest," Clinton said.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, currently on an 11-day, nine-country tour of Europe and Asia, her first overseas trip since taking office, is due in China next week.
On her fifth stop in London on Wednesday, she told reporters consultations were going on with Beijing on whether it was still convenient for her to make the visit.

Former President George Bush, who was ambassador to China from 1974 to 1976 and met Deng in China shortly after becoming U.S. president in 1989, said Deng "played a critical role in establishing strong ties between our two countries."

He said in a statement issued in Houston: "While we were not always in accord, Deng without a doubt made a powerful contribution to a foundation for enduring peace and prosperity in the Asia-Pacific region."
He said he hoped that "Deng Xiaoping's many accomplishments will flourish in China for decades to come and that we all continue to build on his legacy of mutual understanding and respect."

Former President Jimmy Carter, who welcomed Deng to the White House in 1979, called the Chinese leader "an honourable negotiator" and said he always acted "patiently and courageously with the best interests of his people at heart."

"China, the United States and the rest of the world have benefited from Deng's foresight and we owe him a debt of gratitude for the economic progress and increased societal openness that normalised relations have brought," Carter said in a statement issued in Atlanta.
